newsitem.title: USA: Colorado baby girl stricken with E. coli dies.
newsitem.headline: Colorado baby girl stricken with E. coli dies.

text.p: An E. coli outbreak linked to tainted apple juice claimed its first victim on Friday when a 15-month-old girl died in a Denver hospital, a hospital spokeswoman said.
Almost 50 people have fallen sick with the bacterial infection E. coli in the western United States and Canada in the last two weeks, many of them after drinking unpasteurized Odwalla apple juice.
Anna Gimmstad of Greeley, Colorado was pronounced dead at 5:30 a.m. (7:30 a.m. EST) at Children's Hospital. She died of heart and lung failure, spokeswoman Jenny Kolquist said.
The girl drank a lot of apple juice on a recent family trip, but it had not been confirmed if the apple juice was a product from Odwalla Inc., she said.
Tissue samples from the child will be dispatched to the Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in Atlanta, Kolquist said.
The baby, an only child, was brought into the hospital on Oct. 26 and had been listed in critical condition throughout her hospital stay.

If the apple juice was from Odwalla, it would be the first death attributed to juice from the California company. The latest count from the CDC lists 49 cases of E. coli suspected to come from the Odwalla apple juice drink.

Odwalla said it was very saddened to learn of the child's death. The company, based in Half Moon Bay, California, said it was notified by health officials that the child had been associated with the recent E. coli cases linked to Odwalla apple juice.

"On behalf of myself and the people at Odwalla, I want to say how deeply saddened and sorry we are to learn of the loss of this child," Greg Steltenpohl, chairman of Odwalla, said in a statement. "Our hearts go out to the family and our primary concern at this moment is to see that we are doing everything we can to help them," he said.

A Seattle attorney announced on Friday that a lawsuit had been filed against Odwalla and retailer Starbucks Corp. on behalf of a six-year-old boy who required abdominal surgery after being infected with E. coli.
Shares of Odwalla fell sharply on Wall Street following news of the death and the lawsuit.

Odwalla recalled 16 of its products immediately after the first E. coli cases were reported, removing them from store shelves in its distribution region, which covers seven Western states and British Columbia.
On Thursday, the company announced it was reintroducing three juice blends that were reformulated without apple juice.
E. coli seems to present the greatest threat to the very young and the very old, experts say.

Only this week Children's Hospital in Seattle released its remaining E. coli patient after the 2-year-old boy underwent dialysis. On Wednesday five-year-old Brian Dimmock walked out of a Denver area hospital after a two-week hospital stay.

In California, Tara Azizi, 2, remained hospitalized in Children's Hospital Oakland. Azizi was removed from dialysis 24 hours ago and a hospital spokewoman said she did not think Azizi would require a kidney transplant.

The fresh juice from Odwalla is not pasteurized, and the company has said it does not yet know if pasteurization is the best way to insure safety. It has formed a scientific group to study the matter.
